about: Oldest photographs and films, paintings and portraits, cards, stamps and printed ephemera, and scientific instruments and records of the British Isles, each with quoted sources; researched 2026-10-27.

entries.name: Latticed Window at Lacock Abbey
entries.evidence: Henry Fox Talbot made this tiny paper negative of the oriel window in the south gallery of Lacock Abbey with one of his small 'mousetrap' cameras; his note on the mount dates it August 1835. It is in the Science Museum Group collection, kept in the archive of the National Science and Media Museum, Bradford. Niépce's View from the Window at Le Gras (1826-27, France) is an older photograph but not a negative; Wikipedia's articles say 'may be' the earliest surviving negative.

entries.name: Hill & Adamson's Rock House studio
entries.claim: the first photography studio in Scotland
entries.evidence: Robert Adamson moved to Rock House on Calton Hill, Edinburgh, in May 1843 and went into partnership with the painter David Octavius Hill; their calotype portraits and views of 1843-47 are among the earliest photographs of people in Scotland and survive in large numbers, many in the Scottish National Portrait Gallery. Adamson and his circle had already spent about a year making calotypes in St Andrews, so the 'first' is for a studio, not for photography in Scotland.

entries.name: Roundhay Garden Scene
entries.claim: believed to be the oldest surviving film
entries.evidence: Louis Le Prince filmed his family walking in the garden of Oakwood Grange, Roundhay, Leeds, with his single-lens camera on paper film. The original negative is lost; it survives as 20 frames copied on glass plates by the Science Museum in the 1930s. The frame rate (12 or 7 frames a second) is disputed, and some count Janssen's Passage de Vénus series of 1874 as an earlier film.

entries.name: Westminster Retable
entries.claim: the oldest known panel painting in England, and England's oldest altarpiece
entries.evidence: The retable was probably painted for the high altar of Westminster Abbey in the circle of Henry III's court painters. It survived only because it was turned into furniture (by the 1720s it was the top of a cupboard), and much of it is lost; the Hamilton Kerr Institute conserved it from 1998 to 2004. It is now shown in the Abbey's Queen's Diamond Jubilee Galleries.

entries.name: Westminster portrait of Richard II
entries.claim: the earliest known painted portrait of an English monarch
entries.evidence: The over life-size panel shows Richard II enthroned in coronation robes and hangs in the nave of Westminster Abbey; the artist is unknown (André Beauneveu has been suggested). It was restored in 1866, when some of its original gilding and gesso work was removed. Earlier kings appear in effigies, seals and manuscripts, so the claim is for a panel portrait.

entries.name: Wilton Diptych
entries.claim: one of the handful of English panel paintings to survive from the Middle Ages, with a portrait of Richard II
entries.evidence: The small folding altarpiece was painted for Richard II's private devotion and shows him kneeling before the Virgin and Child with his patron saints. Whether its painter was English or French is unknown. It is younger than the Westminster Retable and about the same age as the Westminster portrait of Richard II, so its standing is as a rare survival, not the oldest.

entries.category: Oldest card, stamp or printed ephemera
entries.name: Margery Brews's valentine letter
entries.claim: the earliest surviving valentine letter in English
entries.evidence: Margery Brews of Topcroft, Norfolk, dictated letters to John Paston III in February 1477 calling him her 'right well-beloved Valentine' while their families argued over her dowry; they married later that year. The letters are among the Paston Letters in the British Library. Claims that it is the oldest valentine 'in the world' go further than the sources show; the claim here is for English.

entries.category: Oldest card, stamp or printed ephemera
entries.name: Penny Black
entries.claim: the world's first adhesive postage stamp used in a public postal system
entries.evidence: The Penny Black was introduced with Rowland Hill's uniform penny post and printed until February 1841; tens of millions were printed and many survive. Stamps were sold unofficially before 6 May, and covers postmarked 2 May are known.

sources.quote: The first postage stamp with an adhesive backing was the 1d (one penny) Penny Black, which was put on sale in major post offices in the UK on 1 May 1840

entries.category: Oldest card, stamp or printed ephemera
entries.name: Henry Cole's first Christmas card
entries.claim: the first commercially produced Christmas card
entries.evidence: Henry Cole, later the first director of the V&A, had John Callcott Horsley design the card; about a thousand were printed, and copies sold at a shilling were a commercial flop. The V&A holds a copy. A card by William Maw Egley once thought older was dated 1842 by a misreading; it is from 1848.

entries.name: William Merle's weather diary
entries.claim: the longest and most complete of the earliest weather diaries in Europe, kept in England
entries.evidence: William Merle, a rector in Lincolnshire with ties to Oxford, recorded rainfall, temperature and wind for seven years and wrote two treatises on weather forecasting. His is the longest of the three earliest European weather diaries; a shorter set of daily observations by Roger Bacon from 1269-1270 is older.

entries.name: Central England Temperature record
entries.claim: the longest instrumental record of temperature in the world
entries.evidence: Gordon Manley compiled monthly mean temperatures for the English Midlands from 1659, published in 1953 and 1974; the Met Office keeps the series up to date. Its years before 1722 are mostly given only to the nearest half or whole degree and are pieced together from scattered early records.

entries.name: Newton's reflecting telescope at the Royal Society
entries.age_text: plaque says 1671; probably a later instrument by Newton (or Newton and John Wickens)
entries.claim: not Newton's first reflecting telescope (1668, lost), as its plaque says, but a later one that probably keeps his mirrors
entries.evidence: Newton built the first known reflecting telescope in 1668 and a second in 1671, which he gave to the Royal Society; that one fell apart by 1731 and was lost. The telescope the Society now holds was presented in 1766 by the instrument makers Heath and Wing, and its plaque calls it the first, made in 1671. The Royal Society's catalogue calls it his second model; analysis of its mirror (no silver, some arsenic) suggests a third telescope.
